sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Dhātṛ** (*dhatr*) — The One Who Sets the World — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Creation, Ordinance, Support". The name means "'The Ordainer, the Establisher' (from dhā, to place), an Āditya"[^1].

Dhātṛ is the Vedic verb of creation made personal: "the Establisher," the one who sets the sun in the sky and the child in the womb. Where Brahmā would later be a personality, Dhātṛ is still a function radiant with worship — creation as the act of setting-down.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Dhātṛ** and serves its temple at [dhātṛ.com](https://xn--dht-2oa5868a.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *dhatr* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Brāhmaṇas (Śatapatha, Aitareya, etc.), Sacred Books of the East, 800 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **धातृ**. Etymologically it means "'The Ordainer, the Establisher' (from dhā, to place), an Āditya"[^1].

The ASCII form *dhatr* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Dhātṛ** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **d** → **D** — Same letter
- **h** → **h** — Same letter
- **a** → **ā** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **t** → **t** — Same letter
- **r** → **ṛ** — Script-specific diacritic

The project holds the domain **dhātṛ.com** (xn--dht-2oa5868a.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/d̪ʱɑːˈt̪r̩/** — Sanskrit (IAST).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: dhah-TRUH; the ṛ is a rolled vocalic r.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Devanagari** — धातृ
- **Conventional** — Dhatri
- **Owned form** — Dhātṛ

Sanskrit dhātṛ is an agent noun from the root dhā, "to set, place, establish," with the syllabic ṛ of the nominative — the vowel that is also a consonant, written ऋ. The restoration Dhātṛ keeps both the long ā and the vocalic ṛ that dictionaries print. The syllabic ṛ is a vowel made of the consonant itself: dhātṛ, two syllables, the final one vocalized r.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **धातृ**.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *dhātṛ*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- ध = dha
- आ = ā (long)
- तृ = tṛ (vocalic ṛ)
- dhātṛ is the Āditya of creation and ordinance, "the Establisher"

Written धातृ in Devanagari: dhā with its long vowel mark, then tṛ with the vocalic ṛ sign below. The root dhā underlies a family of cosmic-order words — dhāman (ordinance), dhārman (law), dhātu (element) — and the god is their shared agent.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Dhātṛ is the Vedic verb of creation made personal: "the Establisher," the one who sets the sun in the sky and the child in the womb. Where Brahmā would later be a personality, Dhātṛ is still a function radiant with worship — creation as the act of setting-down.[^1]

### The Setter of Suns

Ṛgveda 10.190: he established heaven and earth, the waters and the light.

### With Vidhātṛ

Paired with the "Disposer" — the Establisher founds, the Disposer assigns each thing its law.

### Dhātu

His root-word: the elements of grammar and of medicine — the set-down units of reality.

### The Womb

He "establishes the embryo" — creation biological as well as cosmic.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Dhātṛ concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The measuring line** — The demarcation by which the formless receives form
- **The lotus seat** — Later iconography's gift to the establishing powers
- **The syllable dhā** — The root as emblem — setting, placing, founding

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Dhātṛ's mythology is the Ṛgveda's creation poetry itself: he appears wherever the text needs not a story but the act — the setting of each thing in its station.[^1]

### Ṛgveda 10.190 (The Ordinance)

The hymn of creation names the sequence: from fervour was born order and truth, from them the night and the ocean; from the ocean the year, apportioning nights and days. "The Establisher (Dhātṛ), as he had made the sun and moon, established heaven and earth, the mid-air and the light" — creation as a series of settings, each thing fixed where it belongs.[^2]

### Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ (The Pair)

The Atharvaveda and Brāhmaṇas pair him with Vidhātṛ, the Disposer: one founds, one assigns — the joint authors of each being's fate, invoked together at marriage and birth rites. A man's fortune, the texts say, is "written on his forehead" by these two: the Indian image of destiny's inscription begins here.

### Becoming Brahmā (The Succession)

In the later literature Dhātṛ's offices pass to Brahmā — the names are used almost interchangeably in the epics, "Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ" becoming a formula for fate itself. It is the quietest succession in religion: the god does not die; his grammar is inherited. Every time the Purāṇas say "as fate ordained," the old Establisher is still at work under his successor's name.

### Written on the Forehead (The Inscription)

The classical image of Indian fate descends from his pair: Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, the texts say, inscribe each child's destiny on the forehead at birth — the lalāṭa-likhitā, the forehead-writing that no effort can erase. The proverb that runs through a thousand stories and films — "what is written will happen" — is his liturgy in miniature: the Establisher has already set down the lines; the drama of life is discovering where they were set.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Comparative philology hears his cognates across the Indo-European family: the root *dheh₁- gives Greek títhēmi ("I set") and English "do" — the Establisher's verb is one of the family's deepest. Within India he merges with Brahmā and, in the Smarta synthesis, with the abstract Brahman: the person dissolves into the principle. The Avestan dātā ("the Law-giver") is his Iranian counterpart in office if not in name.[^1]

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], [[kali|Kālī]], and [[lakshmi|Lakṣmī]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: His root-word dhātu became a foundational term of two civilizations of learning: Pāṇini's grammar organizes Sanskrit as a list of dhātus (verbal roots), and Āyurveda organizes the body as seven dhātus (tissue-elements). "Dhātṛ" survives as a name for fate in the vernaculars; the formula "dhātā-vidhātā" still opens Hindu birth-rite invocations. The idea that grammar and medicine share one word for "the set-down units" is his unnoticed monument.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: An aniconic god leaves no temples: Dhātṛ's material trace is the textual tradition — the Ṛgveda manuscripts (among the world's oldest continuously transmitted texts, UNESCO Memory of the World) and the ritual manuals that prescribe his invocation. The birth-rites (garbhādhāna and jātakarman) where he and Vidhātṛ are called to establish the child's fortune are performed, archaeologically invisible but ethnographically continuous, to this day.[^1]

sections.label: Vedic References
sections.body:
The Establisher's titles are the root declined through its meanings.

- **Dhātṛ** — 'the Establisher'; the agent noun as theonym.
- **Vidhātṛ** — 'the Disposer'; his constant pair, invoked with him at every birth-rite.
- **Prajāpati** — 'Lord of Progeny'; the office his functions pass to.
- **Jagad-dhātṛ** — 'Establisher of the World'; the epic expansion of his name.
- **Dhāman** — 'the Ordinance'; his power as noun, the fixed station of each thing.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda 10.190; Atharvaveda (Dhātṛ-Vidhātṛ hymns).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Upaniṣads
sections.body: The Upaniṣads absorb him almost completely: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's "He who dwells in all beings, whom all beings do not know, who controls all from within" is the Establisher become the inner controller, and the Kaṭha's cosmic order — sun and moon and fire keeping their stations "from fear of him" — is ṚV 10.190's sequence turned inward. Dhātṛ's fate is the Upanishadic movement itself: the god who sets each thing in its place becomes the one Self in whom all places are set.

sources.citation: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.3.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Purāṇas
sections.body: In the Purāṇas his offices pass to Brahmā, and his name survives as a formula: "Dhātā-Vidhātā" — the Establisher and Disposer — is the epic-Purāṇic shorthand for fate itself, invoked at births and lamented at deaths. The Bhāgavata's creator-lists fold him into the Brahmā function; the Mahābhārata uses the pair's names for destiny's inscription on the forehead. The Purāṇic record is thus his apotheosis by absorption: not a god worshipped apart, but the grammar of ordainment that all the worshipped gods obey.

sources.citation: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (creator lists); Mahābhārata (Dhātā-Vidhātā formulae).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Mantras & Stotras
sections.body: His mantra is his own verse: **Ṛgveda 10.190** — the hymn of the ordinance — is recited in the creation-liturgies and the temple foundation rites of the living tradition, the "as he had made the sun and moon" still spoken when things are set in place. The birth-rites (garbhādhāna, jātakarman) invoke Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ by name to establish the child's fortune — the oldest continuously used invocation of his office, four thousand years of "may the Establisher establish."

sources.citation: Ṛgveda 10.190; the jātakarman liturgy.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Dhātṛ is the god of foundations — the moment a thing is set where it will stand. Language, law, the body, the year: all are "establishments" in his grammar. He asks the builder's question beneath every ambition: not what will you make, but where, truly, have you set it down?

His is the least visible and most load-bearing idea in the Veda: that the world holds because things have been set where they belong — the sun in its path, the word in its form, the root in its dhātu. Grammar and medicine, the two great Indian sciences, both took his root-word for their elements, as if to say: reality is well-placed, and knowledge is learning the placements. Every foundation poured, every standard ratified, every definition fixed is a small act of Dhātṛ — the setting-down on which everything else stands.

It is fitting that the Establisher left no image: the act of setting-down is invisible in everything that stands. Languages keep their roots, bodies keep their elements, years keep their months — all establishments, all his. The Ṛgveda's wager is that order is not an accident but an act, performed once and renewed with every thing that is set, placed, founded, or named truly. Every well-laid stone is his unnoticed hymn.

And when the birth-rite is said today and the parents ask for the child to be well-established, the old god is still invoked — unnamed by most who say the words, present in the grammar of the blessing itself. The Establisher's last hiding place is the language, which is where he always lived.[^1]
